2-2-6.title: Types of variables
2-2-6.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Variables are properties that take on different values and are measurable. In research, the role of a variable depends on how it is used in the design.

KEY POINTS
• Independent variable → manipulated by the experimenter.
• Dependent variable → observed/measured outcome.
• Control variable → a potential independent variable held constant during an experiment.
• Quantitative variables → numerical; qualitative variables → qualities/categories.
• Active variables → can be manipulated, changed or controlled experimentally.
• Attribute variables → pre-existing characteristics of the study population.
• Continuous variables → values across a range.
• Discrete variables → distinct values; the source further distinguishes constant, dichotomous and polytomous forms.

NET-RELEVANT TERMINOLOGY
IV, DV, control/extraneous variable, quantitative vs qualitative, active vs attribute, continuous vs discrete.

COMMON TRAP
Do not confuse the independent variable with the dependent variable, and do not confuse a control variable with the outcome being measured. Random assignment is a way of controlling extraneous/confounding variables; it is not the same thing as sampling.

5-MINUTE TEACHING FOCUS
Start with IV → DV, then classify variables using the source's four contrasts: control/extraneous, quantitative/qualitative, active/attribute, continuous/discrete.

MEMORY HOOK
IV = manipulated • DV = measured • Control = held constant • Active = manipulable • Attribute = pre-existing • Continuous = range • Discrete = distinct
2-2-6.deep_learning:
ACADEMIC CORE
Variables are properties that take on different values and are measurable. The supplied PowerWithin material classifies variables through several contrasts.

INDEPENDENT VS DEPENDENT
The independent variable is manipulated by the experimenter. The dependent variable is observed and recorded; its behaviour is treated as depending on the independent variable.

CONTROL / EXTRANEOUS
A control variable is a potential independent variable held constant during an experiment. The source gives temperature and time of day as examples. Ciccarelli & White also emphasizes control of extraneous/confounding variables in experimental research.

QUANTITATIVE VS QUALITATIVE
The PowerWithin source describes quantitative variables in numerical terms and qualitative variables in terms of qualities/categories.

ACTIVE VS ATTRIBUTE
Active variables can be manipulated, changed or controlled experimentally. Attribute variables cannot ordinarily be manipulated or controlled in this way; they reflect pre-existing characteristics of the study population, with age, gender and level of motivation given as examples.

CONTINUOUS VS DISCRETE
Continuous variables exist across a range of values. Discrete variables take distinct values; the source divides these into constant, dichotomous and polytomous forms.

DISTINCTION / CAUTION
A variable's label must be interpreted in the context of the research design. Do not treat “independent” as simply meaning “first” or “dependent” as meaning “less important.” The operational definition of a variable is a separate issue: Ciccarelli & White describes operationalization as specifying the procedures used to control or measure variables.

SOURCE BASIS
• PowerWithin Psychology — Unit 2 Research Methodology and Statistics, identifying variables and types of variables.
• Psychology by Ciccarelli & White (6th ed.) — scientific research and experimental method.
• Psychology: A Self-Teaching Guide — research-methods terminology including independent variable, dependent variable and operational definition.

STUDY RULE
Preserve the source-supported classifications and distinctions. Do not add a classification that is not supported by the supplied material.

2-3-1.title: Ethics in conducting research
2-3-1.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Ethics in conducting research concerns protecting participants and maintaining responsible research practice. The uploaded material places ethics alongside research design and reporting. In practice, ethical conduct requires appropriate consent, protection from avoidable harm, responsible handling of participant information and adherence to applicable professional and institutional standards.

KEY POINTS
• Participant welfare is a central ethical concern.
• Consent and voluntary participation matter.
• Privacy and confidentiality must be protected.
• Research procedures should be scientifically and ethically justified.

SOURCE BASIS
PowerWithin Psychology — Unit 2, Ethics in Conducting and Reporting Research; Paper 1 research/ethics material where applicable.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Ethics is part of the research process itself, not something added only when results are written.

MEMORY CUE
Ethics in conducting research → Participant welfare is a central ethical concern • Consent and voluntary participation matter • Privacy and confidentiality must be protected

2-3-2.title: Ethics in reporting research
2-3-2.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Ethics in reporting research concerns honest and responsible representation of what the study actually found. The source framework places reporting ethics alongside conducting research, so researchers must not distort evidence through fabrication, falsification, plagiarism or misleading presentation. Claims should remain proportionate to the design and data.

KEY POINTS
• Report methods and findings accurately.
• Do not fabricate or falsify data.
• Give appropriate credit to sources and contributors.
• Do not claim more than the evidence supports.

SOURCE BASIS
PowerWithin Psychology — Unit 2, Ethics in Conducting and Reporting Research.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
A statistically significant finding does not justify conclusions that the design cannot support.

MEMORY CUE
Ethics in reporting research → Report methods and findings accurately • Do not fabricate or falsify data • Give appropriate credit to sources and contributors

2-5-1.title: Observation
2-5-1.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Observation is a method in which behavior or events are systematically watched and recorded. The uploaded material and Paper 1 notes distinguish participant and non-participant forms and emphasize its usefulness for studying behavior in natural settings. Observation can provide direct behavioral information but requires clear recording procedures and attention to observer effects and bias.

KEY POINTS
• Behavior is recorded rather than inferred only from self-report.
• Participant and non-participant observation are distinct forms.
• Naturalistic observation can increase ecological relevance.
• Observer bias and limited control are important limitations.

SOURCE BASIS
PowerWithin Psychology — Unit 2 methods; Paper 1 Unit 2 observation-method material; Ciccarelli & White, direct observation.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Observation is not automatically objective; what is noticed and recorded can be influenced by the observer and the recording system.

MEMORY CUE
Observation → Behavior is recorded rather than inferred only from self-report • Participant and non-participant observation are distinct forms • Naturalistic observation can increase ecological relevance

2-5-2.title: Survey
2-5-2.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
The survey method gathers information from people by asking questions about their views or behavior. Baron & Misra describe surveys as useful for obtaining information efficiently from large numbers of people and for tracking changes over time. The Self-Teaching Guide similarly describes surveys as a way to obtain a broad picture of a population.

KEY POINTS
• Surveys can reach large samples efficiently.
• Questions may assess attitudes, opinions or reported behavior.
• Repeated surveys can examine change over time.
• Sampling and question wording affect the quality of conclusions.

SOURCE BASIS
Baron & Misra — Research Methods, Survey Method; Psychology: A Self-Teaching Guide — Survey Method.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
A large survey sample does not by itself guarantee valid conclusions; sampling and measurement quality remain important.

MEMORY CUE
Survey → Surveys can reach large samples efficiently • Questions may assess attitudes, opinions or reported behavior • Repeated surveys can examine change over time

2-5-3.title: Interview
2-5-3.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
An interview is a method of obtaining information through direct questioning. The uploaded PowerWithin material distinguishes structured, unstructured and group interviews. Structured interviews use a fixed schedule and are efficient but less flexible; unstructured interviews use open questions and allow probing, producing richer qualitative data but requiring more time and interviewer skill.

KEY POINTS
• Structured interviews use predetermined questions.
• Unstructured interviews are flexible and allow probing.
• Group interviews/focus groups generate interaction among participants.
• Interviewer skill and bias can affect the data.

SOURCE BASIS
PowerWithin Psychology — Unit 2 Interview Process; Baron & Misra — assessment interviews.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Structured and unstructured interviews should not be treated as interchangeable: they differ in flexibility, data type and standardization.

MEMORY CUE
Interview → Structured interviews use predetermined questions • Unstructured interviews are flexible and allow probing • Group interviews/focus groups generate interaction among participants

2-5-4.title: Questionnaires
2-5-4.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Questionnaires are written or otherwise standardized sets of questions used to collect information from respondents. The uploaded sources place questionnaires within survey research. Their main advantage is efficient collection of comparable responses, while wording, response format, nonresponse and self-report limitations can affect validity.

KEY POINTS
• Questionnaires standardize the questions presented to respondents.
• They are efficient for collecting data from many people.
• Response format influences the kind of data obtained.
• Self-report can be affected by memory, interpretation or socially desirable responding.

SOURCE BASIS
Baron & Misra — Survey Method; PowerWithin Psychology — Survey/Questionnaires.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
A questionnaire is a data-collection instrument; 'survey' is the broader research method or strategy in which questionnaires may be used.

MEMORY CUE
Questionnaires → Questionnaires standardize the questions presented to respondents • They are efficient for collecting data from many people • Response format influences the kind of data obtained

2-5-7.title: Field studies

CORE CONCEPT
Field studies examine behavior in real-world settings rather than only under tightly controlled laboratory conditions. The source framework includes field studies as a distinct research method, and Baron & Misra provide examples of community- and school-based research. Field settings can improve contextual relevance while reducing experimental control.

KEY POINTS
• Research occurs in a natural or real-world setting.
• Contextual information can be richer than in a laboratory.
• Control over extraneous variables is generally lower.
• Interpretation must consider the setting in which the behavior occurred.

SOURCE BASIS

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Field study does not automatically mean qualitative research; field research can use different kinds of data and designs.

2-5-8.title: Cross-cultural studies
2-5-8.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Cross-cultural studies compare psychological phenomena across cultural groups or settings. The uploaded material uses cross-cultural research to show why psychological findings should not automatically be assumed to be culturally universal. Baron & Misra discuss evidence that cultural background can affect developmental patterns and the interpretation of psychological constructs.

KEY POINTS
• The basic purpose is comparison across cultural contexts.
• Culture can influence behavior, development and interpretation.
• Cross-cultural comparisons can reveal limits of generalization.
• Measurement equivalence and cultural context are important concerns.

SOURCE BASIS
PowerWithin Psychology — Unit 2 Cross-Cultural Studies; Baron & Misra — cross-cultural discussion of moral development.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Finding a cultural difference does not by itself establish its cause; cultural groups differ on many correlated conditions.

MEMORY CUE
Cross-cultural studies → The basic purpose is comparison across cultural contexts • Culture can influence behavior, development and interpretation • Cross-cultural comparisons can reveal limits of generalization

Factor-analysis interpretation uses quantities such as factor loadings, eigenvalues, communalities and factor scores to understand the structure extracted from correlated variables. The uploaded PowerWithin material describes a factor loading as the relationship between a variable and factor and an eigenvalue as the variance explained by a factor. Rotation is used to make the output easier to interpret.

KEY POINTS
• Factor loading indicates the relationship of a variable with a factor.
• Eigenvalues represent variance explained by factors.
• Rotation helps make factor patterns more interpretable.
• The source distinguishes exploratory factor analysis from confirmatory factor analysis.

2-15-4.title: Randomized Block Designs
2-15-4.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
A randomized block design groups participants or experimental units into relatively homogeneous blocks on a variable that may influence the outcome, then randomizes treatment conditions within blocks. The supplied Revisathon material includes questions on randomized block ANOVA and error degrees of freedom, while the NET material lists randomized block designs among experimental designs.

KEY POINTS

2-15-8.title: Time series
2-15-8.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Time-series designs collect repeated observations of an outcome across multiple time points. The supplied Paper 1 material places time-series designs within quasi-experimental designs, while the NET material lists time series in its experimental-design coverage. Repeated observations allow researchers to examine patterns before and after an intervention or event.

KEY POINTS
• The same outcome is observed repeatedly across time.
• The sequence of observations is central to interpretation.
• Time-series designs are useful when random assignment is not feasible.
• Pre-intervention and post-intervention patterns can be compared.

SOURCE BASIS
PowerWithin Psychology — Unit 2 Experimental Designs; Paper 1 Unit 2 Time Series Design.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Repeated measurement alone does not establish causality; alternative explanations for changes over time must still be considered.

MEMORY CUE
Time series → The same outcome is observed repeatedly across time • The sequence of observations is central to interpretation • Time-series designs are useful when random assignment is not feasible

2-3-1|CORE IDEA.title: Ethics in conducting research
2-3-1|CORE IDEA.explanation: Ethics in conducting research concerns protecting participants and maintaining responsible research practice. The uploaded material places ethics alongside research design and reporting. In practice, ethical conduct requires appropriate consent, protection from avoidable harm, responsible handling of participant information and adherence to applicable professional and institutional standards.

2-3-2|CORE IDEA.title: Ethics in reporting research
2-3-2|CORE IDEA.explanation: Ethics in reporting research concerns honest and responsible representation of what the study actually found. 2-5-1|CORE IDEA.title: Observation
2-5-1|CORE IDEA.explanation: Observation is a method in which behavior or events are systematically watched and recorded. Observation can provide direct behavioral information but requires clear recording procedures and attention to observer effects and bias.

2-5-2|CORE IDEA.title: Survey
2-5-2|CORE IDEA.explanation: The survey method gathers information from people by asking questions about their views or behavior. Baron & Misra describe surveys as useful for obtaining information efficiently from large numbers of people and for tracking changes over time. The Self-Teaching Guide similarly describes surveys as a way to obtain a broad picture of a population.

2-5-3|CORE IDEA.title: Interview
2-5-3|CORE IDEA.explanation: An interview is a method of obtaining information through direct questioning. The uploaded PowerWithin material distinguishes structured, unstructured and group interviews. Structured interviews use a fixed schedule and are efficient but less flexible; unstructured interviews use open questions and allow probing, producing richer qualitative data but requiring more time and interviewer skill.

The uploaded PowerWithin material describes it as a way to reduce systematic error associated with two blocking dimensions while balancing treatment placement. Each treatment occurs once in every row. Each treatment also occurs once in every column. Rows and columns represent two sources of systematic variation.

2-15-7|CORE IDEA.explanation: Cohort studies follow a defined group of people who share a characteristic or exposure and examine outcomes over time or across relevant conditions. 2-15-8|CORE IDEA.title: Time series
2-15-8|CORE IDEA.explanation: Time-series designs collect repeated observations of an outcome across multiple time points. The supplied Paper 1 material places time-series designs within quasi-experimental designs, while the NET material lists time series in its experimental-design coverage. Repeated observations allow researchers to examine patterns before and after an intervention or event.

2-15-8|KEY FEATURES.title: Time series
2-15-8|KEY FEATURES.explanation: Time-series designs collect repeated observations of an outcome across multiple time points. The supplied Paper 1 material places time-series designs within quasi-experimental designs, while the NET material lists time series in its experimental-design coverage. Repeated observations allow researchers to examine patterns before and after an intervention or event. The same outcome is observed repeatedly across time. The sequence of observations is central to interpretation. Time-series designs are useful when random assignment is not feasible.
